text:
Help me write an announcement to our staff. I'm the COO of a credit union with 7 branches. We're closing the Maple Street and Route 9 branches on March 31 and moving the people who work there to a new member phone and chat center.

Facts:
- The two branches have 14 staff between them. Every one of them is offered a job in the phone and chat center at the same pay or higher.
- Visits to those two branches fell 44% over the last three years. Phone and chat contacts across the credit union went up 60%.
- Members calling us now wait an average of 9 minutes on hold.
- The center will be open 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. on weekdays. The branches were open 9 to 5. Shifts will rotate.
- Staff in the center can work from home two days a week after 90 days of training.
- Anyone who doesn't take the new role gets 2 weeks of pay for every year they've worked here.

I want the announcement to say that this change will make everyone's job better. About 400 words, sent by email from me.

Before I draft it, there's one problem with the main claim.

**What you want to say:** this change will make everyone's job better.

**What your facts support:** the new role pays the same or more, can be done from home two days a week, and sits where member demand is growing (phone and chat contacts up 60%, branch visits down 44%). It also fixes a real problem: members are waiting 9 minutes on hold. All of that supports a claim like *"this is a secure job with real advantages, and it lets us serve members much better."* It doesn't support *"better for everyone."*

**How staff are likely to read the strong version:**
- **"Better for me? I've worked 9 to 5 for years."** The center is open 12 hours a day with rotating shifts, so some people will be working evenings. Your facts don't answer this, and for anyone with childcare or a second job, the change may really be worse.
- **"If it's better, why offer severance?"** Your facts do answer this one. The severance is there for people whose lives don't fit the new schedule. I'd say that plainly in the email.
- **"Is my branch next?"** The other five branches will read "everyone" as including them. Nothing in your facts tells them what changes for them, or whether more closures are coming.

When staff can see that a promise isn't true for them, they tend to doubt the rest of the email too. That includes the parts that are true and that you want them to believe.

**My recommendation:** say the role is secure, pays at least as much and offers remote work. Be open that the hours are changing and that this won't suit everyone, and present the severance as the respectful choice for those people. I can still write the "better for everyone" version if you prefer. You know your staff, so it's your call.

Before I write it, a few facts would make it stronger, and I won't make them up:
1. **Shifts:** how long is each shift, and how often does someone rotate onto evenings?
2. **Other branches:** are more closures planned? If not, can you say so?
3. **Next steps:** when do staff need to decide, when does training start, and who should they talk to?
4. **Branch members:** will anything be in place for them, like ATMs or the nearest branch?

Which version would you like, and what can you tell me about these four points? If you'd rather not wait, I'll write it with placeholders for the missing facts.

Fair point. Go with your version, say what's true.

1. I don't have shift lengths or how often people rotate onto evenings yet. What I can commit to: staff with the most years here pick shifts first. I can't promise anyone 9 to 5.
2. I don't know about the other branches, so leave that out.
3. Written offers by February 14, decision due March 1. Anyone who wants a one-on-one with HR can have one. I don't have a training start date.
4. I don't know what's planned for members yet.

I wrote it the way we agreed. It doesn't promise the job will be better for everyone. It says what's good about the role, is open about the schedule change, and treats the severance as a legitimate choice.

<final_document>
**Subject: Maple Street and Route 9 branches closing March 31: what it means for you**

Team,

I want you to hear this from me first. On March 31 we will close our Maple Street and Route 9 branches. Each of the 14 people who work at those branches will be offered a job in our new member phone and chat center, at the same pay or higher.

**Why we're doing this**

Over the last three years, visits to these two branches fell 44%. Over the same period, phone and chat contacts across the credit union rose 60%. Our members have changed how they reach us, and we haven't kept up. A member who calls us today waits 9 minutes on hold on average. That isn't the service our members deserve. The people best placed to fix it are experienced staff who already know our members and our products.

**What the new role offers**

Everyone at both branches is being offered a role, so no one there loses their job because of this change. Pay will be the same or higher. After 90 days of training, center staff can work from home two days a week. And you'll be working in the part of the credit union that's growing.

**What will be harder**

The center will be open 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. on weekdays, and shifts will rotate. The branches were open 9 to 5, so this means some evening work, and I can't promise anyone a 9-to-5 schedule. We haven't set shift lengths or the rotation pattern yet, and I'll share them as soon as they're decided. What I can promise now is that staff with the most years here will pick their shifts first.

I know this schedule won't work for everyone. If the new role doesn't fit your life, you can turn it down and receive two weeks of pay for every year you've worked here. That's a real option, and no one will think less of anyone who takes it.

**What happens next**

- **By February 14:** everyone at Maple Street and Route 9 will receive a written offer.
- **By March 1:** please let us know your decision.
- **Anytime before then:** if you'd like a one-on-one conversation with HR, you can have one. [How to book.]

To everyone at Maple Street and Route 9: thank you. Closing a branch is hard on the people who built it, and I don't take that lightly. To everyone else: please support your colleagues through this change.

If you have questions, reply to this email or talk to HR.

[Name]
Chief Operating Officer
</final_document>

A few things to check before you send it:

- **Length:** it's about 420 words.
- **Placeholders:** fill in how staff book time with HR, and your name.
- **Questions:** the last line invites replies to you. If you don't want to field those yourself, change it to "talk to HR."
- **Left out on purpose:** the other branches, the training start date and plans for members. If staff at the other five branches are likely to ask whether they're next, decide now what you or their managers will say, even if the answer is "I don't know yet."
- **Shift details:** when the shift lengths and rotation are set, send them in a follow-up before March 1. People will need them to make their decision.
